The Qur'an, 66:1: ﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what God has made lawful for you?﴾ There are two reports concerning its occasion of revelation. One is: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came one day to the house of his wife Hafsa, daughter of Umar ibn al-Khattab, and found that she had gone out to visit her father. So he sent for his slave-girl Maria and had intercourse with her in the house. Then Hafsa came and said: 'O Messenger of God, among your wives there was none more insignificant to you than me. Do you do this in my house and on my bed?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to her, seeking to appease her: 'Would it please you if I forbade her?' She said: 'Yes.' So he said: 'I have forbidden her.'" The other report is: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to enter upon his wife Zaynab bint Jahsh and drink honey with her. Aisha, Hafsa and Sawda bint Zam'a agreed that whoever went in to him should say: 'You have eaten maghafir.' Maghafir is the gum of the 'urfut tree, which is sweet and has an unpleasant smell. They did this, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'No, but I drank honey.' They said: 'Its bees must have grazed on the 'urfut.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'I will never drink it again.' He disliked that an unpleasant odour should be found on him. Afterwards he entered upon Zaynab, and she said: 'Shall I give you some of that?' He said: 'I have no need of it.' So the verse was revealed as a rebuke to him for constricting himself, by forbidding the slave-girl or by forbidding the honey." The first report is more famous, and scholars have discussed the jurisprudence of the sura in light of it. The second was narrated by al-Bukhari and others.

Let us discuss the jurisprudence of prohibition (tahrim). As for forbidding food, wealth and all other things apart from women, it does not bind, and there is nothing due from one who does so according to Malik; Abu Hanifa obligated expiation (kaffara) for it. As for forbidding a slave-girl, if one intends by it emancipation, it binds; if one does not intend that, it does not bind. Its ruling is what we have mentioned regarding food. As for forbidding a wife, people have differed about it in many opinions. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Abbas, Aisha and others said: it only entails the expiation for an oath. Malik, according to the well-known position from him, said: three divorces for one who has consummated the marriage, and for one who has not consummated it, his intention is considered, so he is judged by what he intended, whether one, two or three. Ibn al-Majishun said: it is three in both cases. It is narrated from Malik that it is one irrevocable divorce (ba'in), and it has been said that it is one revocable divorce (raj'i).

﴿seeking the pleasure of your wives﴾, that is, seeking the pleasure of your wives by forbidding what God made lawful for you, meaning his forbidding of the slave-girl in pursuit of Hafsa's pleasure. This indicates that the verse was revealed concerning the forbidding of the slave-girl. As for forbidding the honey, he did not intend by it the pleasure of his wives; he only left it because of its smell. ﴿And God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: in this there is an indication that God forgave him for what He rebuked him for regarding the prohibition, and that His rebuke in this matter was itself an honour to him. The rebuke fell only upon his constricting himself, peace be upon him, and abstaining from what he had a desire for. How wrong was al-Zamakhshari in saying that this was a lapse on his part, because he forbade what God had made lawful, which is a lack of good manners toward the station of prophethood.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 66, verse 2:

﴿Indeed, Allah has prescribed for you the dissolution of your oaths.﴾ At-tahillah (the dissolution of an oath) is the expiation (al-kaffarah), and here the Exalted refers to what was mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah [89] about its description. The scholars differed regarding what is meant by it here. As for the view of those who say that the verse was revealed concerning the prohibition of the slave-girl, then there is difference of opinion on this. Whoever says that the prohibition entails an expiation of oath, cites it as evidence. Whoever says that the prohibition entails a divorce says: the expiation here is only because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ swore and said: "By Allah, I will not approach her ever." As for the view that the verse was revealed concerning the prohibition of honey, there is also difference of opinion. Whoever requires an expiation for prohibiting food says: this expiation is for the prohibition, and whoever says there is no expiation in it says: it is only the expiation because he swore not to drink it. It was also said: it refers to his oath, peace be upon him, that he would not enter upon his wives for a month. ﴿And Allah is your Mawla⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ (protector and helper)⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ It may be that al-Mawla means the Helper (al-Nasir), or the Supreme Master (al-Sayyid al-A'zam).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 66, verse 3:

﴿And when the Prophet confided a matter to one of his wives, a saying (ḥadīth)﴾. Scholars differed about this matter (ḥadīth) into three views. The first: that it was the prohibition of the slave-girl (taḥrīm al-jāriya), for when he prohibited her, he said to Ḥafṣa: "Do not tell anyone about that." The second: that he said, "Abū Bakr and ʿUmar will govern the affair after me." The third: that it was his saying, "I drank honey (shharibtu ʿasalan)." The first is the most well-known. The wife referred to here is Ḥafṣa. ﴿So when she told it, and Allah revealed it to him, he made known part of it and disregarded part of it﴾. Ḥafṣa had informed ʿĀʾisha of what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had confided to her about the prohibition of the slave-girl, and Allah informed His Messenger, peace be upon him, of that. So he rebuked Ḥafṣa for disclosing his secret, and he divorced her. Then Allah commanded him to take her back, and he took her back. It was also said that he did not divorce her. So the phrase "when she told it" has an omitted object, which is ʿĀʾisha. The phrase "Allah revealed it to him" means He informed him of her telling of it. The phrase "he made known part of it" means he reproached Ḥafṣa for part of it, and "disregarded part of it" means out of modesty and generosity, for it is the habit of noble people to overlook faults and to be sparing in reproach. It is also read ʿarrafa (without the doubling), from al-maʿrifa (knowledge). ﴿So when he told her about it, she said, "Who informed you of this?"﴾. That is, when the Prophet ﷺ told Ḥafṣa that she had disclosed his secret, she thought that ʿĀʾisha was the one who had informed him, so she said to him, "Who informed you of this?" When he told her that it was Allah who had informed him, she fell silent and submitted.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 66, verse 4:

﴿If you two turn in repentance to Allah, your hearts have indeed inclined (from the right course)﴾. This is an address to ʿĀʾisha and Ḥafṣa, and (it concerns) their repentance for what occurred between them in the matter of the forbidding of the slave-girl or the honey. The meaning of ﴿ṣaghat﴾ is: they inclined away from the right course. Ibn Masʿūd recited "zāghat" (swerved), and the meaning is: if you repent to Allah, then there has proceeded from you both what necessitates repentance. ﴿And if you two back each other against him, then indeed Allah is his Protector﴾. The meaning is: if you two cooperate against him (ﷺ) by doing what displeases him, such as excessive jealousy and divulging his secret and the like, then he has one who will support him. Here "mawlāhu" (his protector) may mean the Supreme Master, so one stops at "his protector," and Jibrīl is the subject (mubtada') with "ẓahīr" as its predicate and the predicate of what is conjoined to it. It may also mean the supporting ally (walī nāṣir), so Jibrīl is conjoined and connected with what precedes it, and one stops at "ṣāliḥ al-mu'minīn," with "al-malā'ika" as the subject and "ẓahīr" as its predicate. This second reading is more apparent and preferable, for two reasons. The first: the meaning of "supporter" is more fitting in this context, since that is an honour and distinction for the Prophet (ﷺ). If it means "master," then this is shared by the Prophet (ﷺ) with others, because Allah, Exalted is He, is the master of all His creation in that sense, so there is no special distinction for him in it. The second reason: it is reported in the authentic ḥadīth that when this occurred, ʿUmar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what troubles you of the affairs of women? If you have divorced them, then Allah is with you, and His angels, and Jibrīl is with you, and Abū Bakr is with you, and I am with you." So the verse was revealed in agreement with ʿUmar's statement, and his words imply that support is "with you." ﴿And the righteous of the believers﴾. Scholars differed over whether "ṣāliḥ" is singular or a plural with the nūn dropped due to the construct. On the view that it is singular, it refers to Abū Bakr; it was also said to be ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. On the view that it is plural, it is general, covering every righteous person.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 66, verse 5:

﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you﴾ and so on, as support for the Prophet ﷺ. It is related that Umar said this, and the Qur'an came down in agreement with him. Indeed, Umar said to the Prophet ﷺ at that time: "By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, if you were to order me to strike off Hafsah's neck, I would strike it off." We have already explained the meaning of Islam (submission), iman (faith) and qunut (devout obedience). As for al-sa'ihat (the ones who travel), its meaning is "those who fast," as said by Ibn Abbas, and it has been related from the Prophet ﷺ. It was also said that it means "emigrants" (muhajirat), and it was said that it means "those who go toward Allah," because the original sense of siyaha (travelling) is going about on the earth. As for His saying ﴿thayyibat wa abkara﴾ ("previously married and virgins"), some said that what is meant by the virgins here is Maryam daughter of Imran and Asiyah the wife of Pharaoh, for Allah will marry them to the Prophet ﷺ in Paradise; but this requires a sound transmission. The conjunction "wa" (and) is used here for division (taqsim), and if it were dropped the meaning would be disrupted, because previous marriage (thayyubah) and virginity (bakarah) cannot be combined. The Kufans said that it is the "wa" of eight (wāw al-thamāniyah), but that is weak.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 66, verse 6:

﴿Guard yourselves and your families against a Fire﴾ That is: obey Allah, and command your families to obey Him, so that you may protect yourselves and your families through obedience to Him from the Fire. Here he has expressed the effect (musabbab), which is protection from the Fire, by its cause (sabab), which is obedience. ﴿Its fuel is men and stones﴾ This was mentioned in al-Baqarah [24]. ﴿Over it are angels, stern and severe﴾ meaning the guardians of the Fire, and their sternness and severity. It may be intended to refer to their bodies and to the hardness of their hearts. ﴿And they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, but do what they are commanded﴾ It has been said: this is an emphasis on His saying, "they do not disobey Allah." It has also been said: the meaning of "they do not disobey" is carrying out the command, and the meaning of "they do what they are commanded" is their diligence and energy in what they are commanded to do regarding the punishment of people.

Translation:

﴿Do not make excuses today﴾ — meaning, the Day of Resurrection. It is possible that this is an address from God to the disbelievers, or an address from the angels.

**Sincere repentance** (﴿تَوْبَةً نَّصُوحاً﴾). Umar ibn al-Khattab said: Sincere repentance is that you repent from a sin and then never return to it, and you do not wish to return to it. It was also said that its meaning is pure repentance, from the expression "pure honey" (ʿasal nāṣiḥ), meaning honey that has been purified from wax. It was also said that it is that the earth becomes too narrow for the one who repents, despite its vastness, as in the repentance of ﴿the three who were left behind﴾ [al-Tawbah: 118].

Al-Zamakhshari said: Repentance is described as sincere (naṣūḥ) by metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi). Sincerity (al-nuṣḥ) is in reality a quality of those who repent, namely that they give sincere counsel to themselves through repentance. We have discussed repentance in His words, "and repent to Allah all together" (al-Nur: 31).

**﴿On the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet﴾**. The governing element of "the Day" (yawm) may be what precedes it, or what follows it, or an omitted verb whose estimated meaning is "remember." Pausing and beginning differ according to this.

**﴿and those who believed﴾** may be conjunctive to "the Prophet," or it may be a subject whose predicate is ʿabduhu (his servant).

**﴿their light running before them﴾**: this was discussed in al-Hadid [19].

**﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾**: this was discussed in al-Tawbah [88].

The wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. It has been said that the name of Noah's wife was Wahila (al-Wahila) and the name of Lot's wife was Wali'a (al-Wali'a), but this requires authentic transmission.

﴿But they betrayed them﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: the betrayal of Noah's wife was that she used to say that he was mad, and the betrayal of Lot's wife was that she used to inform his people about his guests when they arrived at him. Both of them were, in addition, disbelievers. It has also been said that they betrayed through adultery, but Ibn 'Abbas denied this and said: "No wife of a prophet ever committed adultery," glorifying God and exonerating them from this defect.

God struck a parable with these two women for the disbelievers who had between themselves and the prophets a means of connection; it is as if He is saying: no one avails another anything, even if he is the closest of people to him, like the closeness of Noah's wife and Lot's wife to their husbands. It has also been said that this is an example for the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning what was mentioned at the beginning of the surah, but this is false, because God only struck it for those who disbelieved.

The wife of Pharaoh: her name was Asiya, and she had believed in Moses (peace be upon him). This reached Pharaoh and he ordered her killed, so she made this supplication, and God took her soul. Other accounts of her story have been related, which are lengthy and not authentic.

﴿Deliver me from Pharaoh and his deed﴾: meaning his disbelief and his oppression. It has also been said that it refers to his intercourse with her, but this is weak.

Ibn Juzayy, al-Tashil, on surah 66, verse 12:

﴿Who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into it﴾ means: the private part, which is the organ itself. Her guarding of it is her keeping it and her chastity from every abhorrent thing. ﴿So We breathed into it of Our Spirit﴾ is an expression for Gabriel's breathing into her private part, whereupon God created ʿIsa (ʿalayhi al-salam) in it. God attributed the Spirit to Himself, as the attribution of a created thing to its Creator, and in that there is an honouring of him. ﴿And she affirmed the words of her Lord and His books﴾: "the words of her Lord" may mean the books that God sent down, or His speech with the angels and others. The singular "His book" may mean the Torah, the Gospel, or the genus of books. Abu ʿAmr and Hafs read it in the plural, meaning all the books of God. ﴿Of the devout⁠﻿﻿ ones﴾ means of the worshippers. If it is asked: why did He say "min al-qanitin" with the masculine plural when she is female? The answer: qunut (devotion, ʿibadah) is a quality common to men and women, so the masculine form was given precedence.
